name: jank-with-incidental-framework-error
capturedFrom:
probe/bloc_probe with `--dart-define=scenario=incidental`, Windows desktop target, 2026-08-27. 14-second window covering one full workload cycle: idle, an overflow phase that makes a RenderFlex overflow its parent, three seconds of ordinary work, then a phase that burns 45ms inside build() on every rebuild.

Recorded over loopback rather than on the Android device the other incidents come from, and the reason has been re-established since. Originally it was the transport: events were stamped on receipt, and over adb/WiFi delivery stalled and then flushed -- 111 frame events inside one second, above any refresh rate -- which destroyed the locality this argument rests on. That cause is fixed; events now carry the VM's own clock, and a device re-record confirms it: the overflow arrives live, in order, with clockOffsetMs at -610.

It still belongs on loopback, for a different and more durable reason: the device has no on-budget baseline to argue from. Measured on A015 running this same workload, an ordinary tick costs 14.4ms elapsed against a 16.7ms budget -- 86% of the frame gone before anything goes wrong -- so 44-56% of the frames around the error miss budget anyway, at a mean 21.0ms elapsed for only 12.1ms of build and 6.6ms of raster. On desktop the same ticks build in 3.5ms and the window either side of the error is clean. The claim being pinned here is that frames at the moment of the error were healthy; a target with 2ms of headroom cannot demonstrate that about anything, so re-recording there would weaken the incident rather than strengthen it.
why:
The right answer is `jank`, even though the session contains an exception, and that is the entire point of recording it. `exception present` is not `exception is the root cause`.

What the exception is. Seven `Flutter.Error` events, all the identical text `A RenderFlex overflowed by 390 pixels on the bottom.` — a layout complaint that a box did not fit. It arrives on the same stream, in the same category, at the same severity `error` as a crash would. Nothing about its category distinguishes it. What does distinguish it is in the payload: `hasStack: false`, no `stackTrace` field at all. It names no line of code, because no application code threw.

Why it is not causal, from the events rather than from what an overflow is. The live one, exc_00101, arrived 7.81s after connect. In the engine's own 3-second correlation window either side of it there are 50 frames and *not one of them missed budget* — the slowest is 15.87ms against a 16.67ms budget. The first janky frame after the error comes 3.69s later, outside that window. If the overflow were causing frames to drop, the frames it is sitting in the middle of are where that would show, and they are clean.

Why jank is causal. 27 of 82 frames (32.9%) blew budget, and 26 of those 27 fall in a contiguous three-second block. They are build-bound and not marginally so: janky frames average 45.91ms of build against 0.83ms of raster, while the frames around them average 3.78ms of build. That is a twelve-fold separation between two populations in the same session, and the expensive population is a solid block of time rather than scattered noise. The worst, frm_00213 at 52.71ms (build 50.82, raster 0.78), must be cited: a jank verdict that does not hand back its own worst frame cannot be checked.

What this incident is guarding. Before it, `exceptionHypothesis` carried priority 3 unconditionally, so any exception outranked any performance pattern regardless of what either was made of, and this session was answered `exception` at 0.7 confidence with the overflow named as the root cause — while a 45ms build sat there unmentioned except as an alternative. Confidently wrong, in the specific way this project treats as the expensive failure: it sends a reader to a layout box when the fault is a build. The ranking now depends on whether the exception carries a stack, which is the one discriminator actually present in the captured payload — `library` and `type` are identical between this event and a genuine crash.

Note the asymmetry that keeps this honest. The exception is demoted, not discarded: it stays in `alternativeCauses`, and in a session where nothing else fires it is still the primary hypothesis. The overflow is a real defect worth fixing. It is just not the reason the app stuttered.

limitations: No network evidence in this session. HTTP capture is pull-on-demand and Dart-side only — platform-code and WebView traffic is never visible.
No memory samples captured. Call get_memory, or open the dashboard, to include memory in future diagnoses.
VM timeline events are fetched on demand and not stored, so they take no part in correlation.
Only Dart-side runtime state is observed. A cause in platform (Kotlin/Swift) code or in a WebView cannot appear here.

confidenceBreakdown.basis: Conservative heuristic scored from corroborating evidence, not a calibrated probability. Below 0.7 the status is "unknown" rather than a guess.

recommendedFixes: Add a null/bounds guard or try/catch at the failing call site shown in the stack trace.

performance.summary: 27/82 frames (33%) exceeded the 16.67ms budget. Worst 52.71ms, p99 52.71ms. Dominated by the build phase.

findings.claim: 389 widget rebuild(s) across 82 frame(s). Busiest: Text at bloc_probe/lib/main.dart:373 — 27 rebuild(s) over 27 frame(s).
findings.fix: Narrow the rebuild scope around Text at bloc_probe/lib/main.dart:373. Split the widget so only the part that depends on changing state rebuilds, add const constructors, and move computation out of build().

findings.claim: Janky frames spend most of their time building: mean build 45.91ms vs raster 0.83ms.
findings.fix: Build-phase heavy: move expensive work out of build(), use const widgets, cache computed values, and narrow the rebuild scope with smaller widgets or selectors.

recommendedFixes: Narrow the rebuild scope around Text at bloc_probe/lib/main.dart:373. Split the widget so only the part that depends on changing state rebuilds, add const constructors, and move computation out of build().
Build-phase heavy: move expensive work out of build(), use const widgets, cache computed values, and narrow the rebuild scope with smaller widgets or selectors.
limitations: No CPU sampling. A slow build can be attributed to a widget, but not to a specific function — use the DevTools CPU profiler for that.
GC events are not observable: the VM timeline is fetched on demand and not stored, so garbage-collection pauses cannot be ruled in or out.
Frames are only captured while connected, and older ones roll out of the retention window.
State changes are counted, never read: neither Riverpod nor Provider exposes values or provider names through the VM Service, so no claim is made about which provider is responsible.
Rebuild totals cover the busiest locations in each frame, not every rebuild — the long tail is counted but not itemised.
App-versus-package attribution is a path heuristic: getPubRootDirectories is empty until a DevTools client sets it, so there is no authoritative project root.
Only 82 frames in the sample — treat the percentiles as indicative.

notes: No route changes captured. Navigator posts Flutter.Navigation on push/pop, so either nothing has navigated since connecting, or the app is a release build.
5 frame(s) rebuilt more locations than are retained; totals cover the busiest locations per frame, not every rebuild.
